title: Stop letting LLMs predict stock prices directly: Why isolating math from agent reasoning is the only viable architecture
author: OpenComplaint524
selftext:
Over the past year, we've seen dozens of repos claiming to be "AI Hedge Funds" by feeding 10-K filings and price charts directly into GPT-4 or Claude and asking "Should I buy or sell?"

Unsurprisingly, almost all of them blow up on real or out-of-sample data. Why?

1. \*\*Hallucinated Arithmetic\*\*: LLMs are probabilistic language models, not floating-point calculation engines. They will hallucinate moving averages and support levels with 100% confidence.
2. \*\*Sycophancy (Echo Chamber)\*\*: A single agent prompted to analyze an asset will generate a plausible thesis and reinforce its own bias.
3. \*\*Latency & Slippage Disconnect\*\*: Waiting 3 to 10 seconds for an LLM response during volatile price swings guarantees execution slippage.

After building and open-sourcing our multi-agent quantitative framework, we adopted one strict iron rule:

\*\*"Models reason, software calculates."\*\*

Here is what actually makes agentic trading work without blowing up:

\- \*\*Zero-Hallucination Deterministic Math\*\*: All 158 quantitative factors (Alpha158) and rolling statistical moments are computed in vectorized native Python—never by an LLM.

\- \*\*Adversarial Groupthink Breaking\*\*: We isolate 7 investor personas in parallel without cross-talk, then pit the strongest Bull and strongest Bear against each other in a fact-grounded cross-debate.

\- \*\*Absolute Risk Veto (CRO)\*\*: The Chief Risk Officer must hold hardcoded, irreversible 0% allocation veto power over the lead portfolio manager.

\- \*\*Dual-Speed Sentinel\*\*: A 15-minute deliberation loop paired with an independent 10-second lightweight watchdog that adjusts ATR breathing stop-losses without waiting for LLM tokens.

For those running algorithmic or quantitative systems: how are you currently enforcing strict architectural boundaries between LLM semantic extraction and mathematical execution? Would love to hear alternative approaches.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The dual-speed design creates a state-ownership problem worth making explicit. What happens if the 10-second watchdog widens an ATR breathing stop while the 15-minute deliberation loop is closing or reversing the same position? I’d give the watchdog authority only to reduce exposure, never loosen protection, and require versioned position snapshots plus compare-and-swap updates so stale decisions fail safely. The CRO’s irreversible 0% allocation veto should also be enforced below the agent layer, where neither the lead PM nor a delayed order can restore exposure.

replies.author: OpenComplaint524
replies.body:
You hit on the exact concurrency and state-ownership nightmares we had to engineer around. Here is how Lumina's actual code handles all three points you raised:



1. \*\*Watchdog is strictly monotonic (cannot widen stops)\*\*:

In our \`patrol\_positions\` engine, the watchdog is physically forbidden from loosening protection. It only runs ratchet logic:

\- \`peak\_price = max(peak\_price, cur\_price)\` (only tracks upward)

\- Partial take-profit (+10%) moves stop-loss strictly upward to breakeven (\`entry\_price\`).

\- Trailing stop triggers an immediate market exit on a -4% drawdown from peak.

There is literally zero code path allowing the sentinel to widen an ATR floor or increase allocation. It can ONLY de-risk or exit.



2. \*\*Decoupled execution & Fail-Safe race handling\*\*:

The 15-minute deliberation loop and the 10-second watchdog both route exits through the underlying broker engine. If the watchdog closes a position at second 12 while the 15-minute council is still thinking, the position quantity on the broker ledger drops to zero. When the council's delayed ticket hits the broker layer, it immediately fails the ledger balance check and aborts safely (no-op). 

That said, your point about \*\*versioned snapshots and CAS (Compare-and-Swap)\*\* is a much cleaner distributed pattern than relying on broker-side ledger validation—adding explicit position version IDs to our SQLite state is a brilliant improvement we're adopting!



3. \*\*CRO veto lives strictly BELOW the agent layer\*\*:

This is our core rule. Even if the LLM council hallucinates a unanimous 100% BUY, deterministic Python code directly wrapping the broker gateway intercepts the ticket and runs hard checks:

\- Excludes tickers within 3 days of earnings announcements.

\- Hard-rejects any stock trading below its 200-day SMA (Weinstein Stage 4 knife).

\- Freezes execution if Deep OFI (10-level order book) detects spoofing/flash cancellations.

\- Caps sizing via Half-Kelly and correlation spike brakes.



The models only produce hypotheses; cold, unyielding Python math at the socket layer holds the actual keys to execution.



Really appreciate this caliber of systems-level feedback! 👊

comments.author: OldPerformance432
comments.body: The separation between the 15 minute reasoning loop and the 10 second risk watchdog is probably the most interesting architectural choice here. I'd be careful about what happens when they issue conflicting instructions during a fast market move. I use Moon to make my own directional wagers but I'd never want an AI model improvising position sizing or calculating risk from memory. Deterministic execution makes much more sense.

replies.author: OpenComplaint524
replies.body:
100% this. "Never let an LLM do arithmetic with real capital" was rule #0 when building this. 



LLMs are brilliant at qualitative synthesis (e.g. cross-referencing earnings call transcripts with supply chain bottlenecks), but the second you let a model hallucinate a stop distance or "feel" its way into position sizing, you end up with compounding gambler's ruin and rationalized averaging-down.



Our execution layer below the agents is entirely deterministic Python:

1. \*\*Position sizing\*\*: Strictly governed by a Half-Kelly Criterion capped against a Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP) covariance matrix. The LLM can express 99% conviction, but the sizing math will physically cap allocation to sub-single-digit portfolio percent if correlation or volatility runs hot.

2. \*\*Fast-market conflicts\*\*: The 10-second watchdog runs strictly monotonic tightening. If a flash drop triggers the trailing stop, the broker position goes to 0 immediately via IBKR bracket. When the 15-minute deliberation loop eventually wraps up, its stale exit/reversal attempts cleanly no-op against a zero-position check before dispatching.

3. \*\*Hard vetoes\*\*: An earnings blackout window (T-3 to T+3), a 200 SMA stage-4 filter, and Rama Cont OFI spoof detection can completely abort a BUY signal without the LLM ever being consulted.



Directional thesis from reasoning models + zero-discretion deterministic guardrails is the only way we could sleep at night running this on real capital.

comments.author: Illustrious_Ad7630
comments.body:
I think you are on a good path, but personally, I would use LLMs. Even if you are making seven different personalities, it just generates more noise. In your workflow, I feel an alternative database is missing which defines what your 158 math factors mean, instead of giving this information to LLMs.

You need to think of a situation where you have 158 factors; if they are just textbook factors, LLMs will use the data they were fed, which is not necessarily correct, and make seven random personas of questionable information. If a few of the factors are more niche or custom-made, LLMs will fill the void with assumptions based on the name of the factor.

replies.author: OpenComplaint524
replies.body:
Spot on. This is probably the sharpest and most grounded critique in this entire thread, and you hit the exact failure mode of naive "LLM trading" setups.



To clear up how Lumina actually handles this under the hood (because feeding raw 158-factor floats into a context window is indeed pure hallucination fuel):



1. \*\*Alpha158 is calculated & scored deterministically by LightGBM, NOT the LLM:\*\*

   The 158 quantitative features (from Microsoft's Qlib) are computed in pure NumPy/Pandas and evaluated strictly via an offline-trained GBDT / LightGBM tabular pipeline. The LLM never sees the raw 158-dimensional feature matrix or does floating-point math.



2. \*\*What the LLM actually receives (Distilled SHAP, not raw factors):\*\*

   Instead of raw factor tokens, the quantitative engine passes only top-k SHAP feature attributions and normalized z-scores (e.g., \`Factor \[Vol\_ZScore\]: -1.4 (Low vol regime), Momentum\_Rank: 92nd percentile\`).



3. \*\*Division of Labor (Qualitative vs. Quantitative):\*\*

   The LLM agents are strictly forbidden from "predicting prices." Their entire role is qualitative sanity-checking:

   \- Parsing SEC Form 4 insider transactions

   \- Analyzing earnings call transcript sentiment

   \- Checking OpenBB FRED macroeconomic regime changes

   They evaluate whether the macro/qualitative narrative contradicts the quantitative alpha signal.



4. \*\*Your point on Factor Ontology / Dictionary is gold:\*\*

   Your observation about the lack of an underlying factor schema/ontology is brilliant. If an agent interprets \`trend\_strength\_30d\` without knowing the exact mathematical formulation (or whether it's mean-reverting vs. momentum), it risks hallucinating an inverted correlation. 

   

   We're currently designing v6.4, and based on your comment, we're officially adding a \*\*Factor Metadata Schema\*\* (defining mathematical formulas, normalization bounds, and directional semantics) into the agent's function definitions before they ingest SHAP features.



Really appreciate this kind of deep-dive pushback—this is the exact difference between toy prompt wrappers and resilient production architecture.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I agree with the split, and the main thing I'd add is a hard boundary in code. The model can only output a tag or a score from a fixed list, and the software decides size and exits, so a made-up number can never reach an order. I'd also check that the debate and persona layers earn their place. Run the system with and without them on the same period, and keep them only if the results improve out of sample. Cymetica's Event Cards use a similar idea, where the news reading gets a sourced report and the trade itself is a basket of real stocks.

replies.author: OpenComplaint524
replies.body:
100% aligned with this. You summarized the exact principle that keeps LLMs from blowing up accounts: \*\*hard deterministic boundaries in code.\*\*



\*\*1. Our "No Free-Form Quantities" Boundary:\*\*

In our execution engine, the LLM is physically blocked from proposing share quantities, dollar amounts, or price limits. 

Its schema (enforced via Pydantic / strict JSON mode) only accepts:

\- Direction tags: \`Literal\["ACCUMULATE", "HOLD", "TRIM", "LIQUIDATE"\]\`

\- Confidence score: \`float \[0.0 - 1.0\]\`



The entire sizing pipeline is deterministic Python downstream:

\`Position Size = (Account Equity \* Max Risk Limit) / (ATR\_14d \* Volatility\_Multiplier)\`

An LLM can never hallucinate a fat-finger \\$500k market buy, because the sizing function simply ignores what the LLM "feels" the size should be.



\*\*2. The Ablation Study challenge (Do personas earn their keep?):\*\*

This is a fantastic challenge. The multi-persona debate (especially having an aggressive bear like Burry argue against a trend-follower) is great for preventing confirmation bias on high-conviction momentum setups, but in quiet low-vol regimes, it can easily devolve into noisy circular paralysis.

Running a rigorous out-of-sample (OOS) ablation study—comparing raw single-prompt pass-through vs. full multi-agent consensus vs. pure LightGBM baseline—is something we need to formalize. If an agent persona doesn't improve the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio or tail-risk drawdown, it should be pruned.



\*\*3. Cymetica Event Cards:\*\*

Really appreciate the pointer to Cymetica's approach. Decoupling "unstructured text digestion into sourced event primitives" from "execution across a liquid basket" is the right mental model for modern AI systems.



Thanks for grounding the discussion in real engineering discipline!
